# parity_scale_codec - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/parity-scale-codec/^3.7.5/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#parity-scale-codec)Parity SCALE Codec

Rust implementation of the SCALE (Simple Concatenated Aggregate Little-Endian) data format for types used in the Parity Substrate framework.

SCALE is a light-weight format which allows encoding (and decoding) which makes it highly suitable for resource-constrained execution environments like blockchain runtimes and low-power, low-memory devices.

It is important to note that the encoding context (knowledge of how the types and data structures look) needs to be known separately at both encoding and decoding ends. The encoded data does not include this contextual information.

To get a better understanding of how the encoding is done for different types,
take a look at the [“Type encoding (SCALE)” page in Substrate docs](https://docs.substrate.io/reference/scale-codec/).

[§](https://docs.rs#implementation)Implementation

The codec is implemented using the following traits:

[§](https://docs.rs#encode)Encode

The `Encode` trait is used for encoding of data into the SCALE format. The `Encode` trait
contains the following functions:

- `size_hint(&self) -> usize`: Gets the capacity (in bytes) required for the encoded data. This is to avoid double-allocation of memory needed for the encoding. It can be an estimate and does not need to be an exact number. If the size is not known, even no good maximum, then we can skip this function from the trait implementation. This is required to be a cheap operation, so should not involve iterations etc.
- `encode_to<T: Output>(&self, dest: &mut T)`: Encodes the value and appends it to a destination buffer.
- `encode(&self) -> Vec<u8>`: Encodes the type data and returns a slice.
- `using_encoded<R, F: FnOnce(&[u8]) -> R>(&self, f: F) -> R`: Encodes the type data and executes a closure on the encoded value. Returns the result from the executed closure.

**Note:** Implementations should override `using_encoded` for value types and `encode_to` for
allocating types. `size_hint` should be implemented for all types, wherever possible. Wrapper
types should override all methods.

[§](https://docs.rs#decode)Decode

The `Decode` trait is used for deserialization/decoding of encoded data into the respective
types.

- `fn decode<I: Input>(value: &mut I) -> Result<Self, Error>`: Tries to decode the value from SCALE format to the type it is called on. Returns an- `Err`if the decoding fails.

[§](https://docs.rs#compactas)CompactAs

The `CompactAs` trait is used for wrapping custom types/structs as compact types, which makes
them even more space/memory efficient. The compact encoding is described [here](https://docs.substrate.io/reference/scale-codec/#fn-1).

- `encode_as(&self) -> &Self::As`: Encodes the type (self) as a compact type. The type- `As`is defined in the same trait and its implementation should be compact encode-able.
- `decode_from(_: Self::As) -> Result<Self, Error>`: Decodes the type (self) from a compact encode-able type.

[§](https://docs.rs#hascompact)HasCompact

The `HasCompact` trait, if implemented, tells that the corresponding type is a compact
encode-able type.

[§](https://docs.rs#encodelike)EncodeLike

The `EncodeLike` trait needs to be implemented for each type manually. When using derive, it is
done automatically for you. Basically the trait gives you the opportunity to accept multiple
types to a function that all encode to the same representation.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage-examples)Usage Examples

Following are some examples to demonstrate usage of the codec.

[§](https://docs.rs#simple-types)Simple types

```
use parity_scale_codec::{Encode, Decode};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Encode, Decode)]
enum EnumType {
    #[codec(index = 15)]
    A,
    B(u32, u64),
    C {
        a: u32,
        b: u64,
    },
}
let a = EnumType::A;
let b = EnumType::B(1, 2);
let c = EnumType::C { a: 1, b: 2 };
a.using_encoded(|ref slice| {
    assert_eq!(slice, &b"\x0f");
});
b.using_encoded(|ref slice| {
    assert_eq!(slice, &b"\x01\x01\0\0\0\x02\0\0\0\0\0\0\0");
});
c.using_encoded(|ref slice| {
    assert_eq!(slice, &b"\x02\x01\0\0\0\x02\0\0\0\0\0\0\0");
});
let mut da: &[u8] = b"\x0f";
assert_eq!(EnumType::decode(&mut da).ok(), Some(a));
let mut db: &[u8] = b"\x01\x01\0\0\0\x02\0\0\0\0\0\0\0";
assert_eq!(EnumType::decode(&mut db).ok(), Some(b));
let mut dc: &[u8] = b"\x02\x01\0\0\0\x02\0\0\0\0\0\0\0";
assert_eq!(EnumType::decode(&mut dc).ok(), Some(c));
let mut dz: &[u8] = &[0];
assert_eq!(EnumType::decode(&mut dz).ok(), None);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#compact-type-with-hascompact)Compact type with HasCompact

```
use parity_scale_codec::{Encode, Decode, Compact, HasCompact};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Encode, Decode)]
struct Test1CompactHasCompact<T: HasCompact> {
    #[codec(compact)]
    bar: T,
}
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Encode, Decode)]
struct Test1HasCompact<T: HasCompact> {
    #[codec(encoded_as = "<T as HasCompact>::Type")]
    bar: T,
}
let test_val: (u64, usize) = (0u64, 1usize);
let encoded = Test1HasCompact { bar: test_val.0 }.encode();
assert_eq!(encoded.len(), test_val.1);
assert_eq!(<Test1CompactHasCompact<u64>>::decode(&mut &encoded[..]).unwrap().bar, test_val.0);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#type-with-compactas)Type with CompactAs

```
use serde_derive::{Serialize, Deserialize};
use parity_scale_codec::{Encode, Decode, Compact, HasCompact, CompactAs, Error};
#[cfg_attr(feature = "std", derive(Serialize, Deserialize, Debug))]
#[derive(PartialEq, Eq, Clone)]
struct StructHasCompact(u32);
impl CompactAs for StructHasCompact {
    type As = u32;
    fn encode_as(&self) -> &Self::As {
        &12
    }
    fn decode_from(_: Self::As) -> Result<Self, Error> {
        Ok(StructHasCompact(12))
    }
}
impl From<Compact<StructHasCompact>> for StructHasCompact {
    fn from(_: Compact<StructHasCompact>) -> Self {
        StructHasCompact(12)
    }
}
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Encode, Decode)]
enum TestGenericHasCompact<T> {
    A {
        #[codec(compact)] a: T
    },
}
let a = TestGenericHasCompact::A::<StructHasCompact> {
    a: StructHasCompact(12325678),
};
let encoded = a.encode();
assert_eq!(encoded.len(), 2);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#derive-attributes)Derive attributes

The derive implementation supports the following attributes:

- `codec(dumb_trait_bound)`: This attribute needs to be placed above the type that one of the trait should be implemented for. It will make the algorithm that determines the to-add trait bounds fall back to just use the type parameters of the type. This can be useful for situation where the algorithm includes private types in the public interface. By using this attribute, you should not get this error/warning again.
- `codec(skip)`: Needs to be placed above a field or variant and makes it to be skipped while encoding/decoding.
- `codec(compact)`: Needs to be placed above a field and makes the field use compact encoding. (The type needs to support compact encoding.)
- `codec(encoded_as = "OtherType")`: Needs to be placed above a field and makes the field being encoded by using- `OtherType`.
- `codec(index = 0)`: Needs to be placed above an enum variant to make the variant use the given index when encoded. By default the index is determined by counting from- `0`beginning wth the first variant.
- `codec(encode_bound)`,- `codec(decode_bound)`and- `codec(mel_bound)`: All 3 attributes take in a- `where`clause for the- `Encode`,- `Decode`and- `MaxEncodedLen`trait implementation for the annotated type respectively.
- `codec(encode_bound(skip_type_params))`,- `codec(decode_bound(skip_type_params))`and- `codec(mel_bound(skip_type_params))`: All 3 sub-attributes take in types as arguments to skip trait derivation of the corresponding trait, e.g. T in- `codec(encode_bound(skip_type_params(T)))`will not contain a- `Encode`trait bound while- `Encode`is being derived for the annotated type.

[§](https://docs.rs#known-issues)Known issues

Even though this crate supports deserialization of arbitrarily sized array (e.g. `[T; 1024 * 1024 * 1024]`)
using such types is not recommended and will most likely result in a stack overflow. If you have a big
array inside of your structure which you want to decode you should wrap it in a `Box`, e.g. `Box<[T; 1024 * 1024 * 1024]>`.

License: Apache-2.0

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Compact](https://docs.rs/struct.Compact.html)
- Compact-encoded variant of T. This is more space-efficient but less compute-efficient.
- [Compact](https://docs.rs/struct.CompactRef.html)- Ref
- Compact-encoded variant of &’a T. This is more space-efficient but less compute-efficient.
- [Counted](https://docs.rs/struct.CountedInput.html)- Input
- A wrapper for `Input`which tracks the number fo bytes that are successfully read.
- [Decode](https://docs.rs/struct.DecodeFinished.html)- Finished
- A zero-sized type signifying that the decoding finished.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- Error type.
- [IoReader](https://docs.rs/struct.IoReader.html)
- Wrapper that implements Input for any `Read`type.
- [MemTracking](https://docs.rs/struct.MemTrackingInput.html)- Input
- `Input`implementation that can be used for limiting the heap memory usage while decoding.
- [Option](https://docs.rs/struct.OptionBool.html)- Bool
- Shim type because we can’t do a specialised implementation for `Option<bool>`directly.
- [Ref](https://docs.rs/struct.Ref.html)
- Reference wrapper that implement encode like any type that is encoded like its inner type.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Codec](https://docs.rs/trait.Codec.html)
- Trait that allows zero-copy read/write of value-references to/from slices in LE format.
- [Compact](https://docs.rs/trait.CompactAs.html)- As
- Allow foreign structs to be wrap in Compact
- [Compact](https://docs.rs/trait.CompactLen.html)- Len
- Something that can return the compact encoded length for a given value.
- [Decode](https://docs.rs/trait.Decode.html)
- Trait that allows zero-copy read of value-references from slices in LE format.
- [Decode](https://docs.rs/trait.DecodeAll.html)- All
- Extension trait to `Decode`
- [Decode](https://docs.rs/trait.DecodeLength.html)- Length
- Trait that allows the length of a collection to be read, without having to read and decode the entire elements.
- [Decode](https://docs.rs/trait.DecodeLimit.html)- Limit
- Extension trait to `Decode`
- [Decode](https://docs.rs/trait.DecodeWithMemLimit.html)- With - MemLimit
- Extension trait to `Decode`
- [Decode](https://docs.rs/trait.DecodeWithMemTracking.html)- With - MemTracking
- Marker trait used for identifying types that call the `Input::on_before_alloc_mem`
- [Encode](https://docs.rs/trait.Encode.html)
- Trait that allows zero-copy write of value-references to slices in LE format.
- [Encode](https://docs.rs/trait.EncodeAppend.html)- Append
- Trait that allows to append items to an encoded representation without decoding all previous added items.
- [Encode](https://docs.rs/trait.EncodeAsRef.html)- AsRef
- Something that can be encoded as a reference.
- [Encode](https://docs.rs/trait.EncodeLike.html)- Like
- A marker trait that tells the compiler that a type encode to the same representation as another type.
- [Full](https://docs.rs/trait.FullCodec.html)- Codec
- Trait that bound `EncodeLike`along with`Codec`. Usefull for generic being used in function with`EncodeLike`parameters.
- [Full](https://docs.rs/trait.FullEncode.html)- Encode
- Trait that bound `EncodeLike`along with`Encode`. Usefull for generic being used in function with`EncodeLike`parameters.
- [HasCompact](https://docs.rs/trait.HasCompact.html)
- Trait that tells you if a given type can be encoded/decoded in a compact way.
- [Input](https://docs.rs/trait.Input.html)
- Trait that allows reading of data into a slice.
- [Joiner](https://docs.rs/trait.Joiner.html)
- Trait to allow itself to be serialised into a value which can be extended by bytes.
- [Keyed](https://docs.rs/trait.KeyedVec.html)- Vec
- Trait to allow itself to be serialised and prepended by a given slice.
- [Output](https://docs.rs/trait.Output.html)
- Trait that allows writing of data.
- [Wrapper](https://docs.rs/trait.WrapperTypeDecode.html)- Type - Decode
- A marker trait for types that can be created solely from other decodable types.
- [Wrapper](https://docs.rs/trait.WrapperTypeEncode.html)- Type - Encode
- A marker trait for types that wrap other encodable type.

- A tuple struct which can be converted into a `Location`of`parents`value 1 with the inner interior.
- [Persisted](https://docs.rs/struct.PersistedValidationData.html)- Validation - Data

# cumulus_primitives_parachain_inherent - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cumulus-primitives-parachain-inherent/^0.26.0/

## Expand description

Cumulus parachain inherent

The [ ParachainInherentData](https://docs.rs/struct.ParachainInherentData.html) is the data that is passed by the collator to the parachain
runtime. The runtime will use this data to execute messages from other parachains/the relay
chain or to read data from the relay chain state. When the parachain is validated by a parachain
validator on the relay chain, this data is checked for correctness. If the data passed by the
collator to the runtime isn’t correct, the parachain candidate is considered invalid.

To create a [ ParachainInherentData](https://docs.rs/struct.ParachainInherentData.html) for a specific relay chain block, there exists the

`ParachainInherentDataExt` trait in `cumulus-client-parachain-inherent` that helps with this.## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [v0](https://docs.rs/v0/index.html)
- Legacy ParachainInherentData that is kept around for backward compatibility.
Can be removed once we can safely assume that parachain nodes provide the
`relay_parent_descendants`and`collator_peer_id`fields.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Hashed](https://docs.rs/struct.HashedMessage.html)- Message
- An inbound message whose content was hashed.
- [Message](https://docs.rs/struct.MessageQueueChain.html)- Queue - Chain
- This struct provides ability to extend a message queue chain (MQC) and compute a new head.
- [Parachain](https://docs.rs/struct.ParachainInherentData.html)- Inherent - Data
- The inherent data that is passed by the collator to the parachain runtime.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [INHERENT_](https://docs.rs/constant.INHERENT_IDENTIFIER.html)- IDENTIFIER
- [PARACHAIN_](https://docs.rs/constant.PARACHAIN_INHERENT_IDENTIFIER_V0.html)- INHERENT_ - IDENTIFIER_ - V0
- The identifier for the parachain inherent.

- Evaluate `$x:expr`and if not true return`Err($y:expr)`.

- Simple macro to explicitly implement [EnsureOriginWithArg](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.EnsureOriginWithArg.html)to be used on any type which implements[EnsureOrigin](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.EnsureOrigin.html). This is quick and dirty, so you must use the type parameters`O`(the origin type),`T`(the argument type) and`AccountId`(if you are using the`O: ..`form).

- [match_](https://docs.rs/macro.match_types.html)- types
- Create a type which implements the `Contains`trait for a particular type with syntax similar to`matches!`.

- Print out a formatted message.

- Enable/disable the given code depending on
`feature = "std"`being enabled for the crate or not.

## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [derive_](https://docs.rs/attr.derive_impl.html)- impl
- This attribute can be used to derive a full implementation of a trait based on a local partial impl and an external impl containing defaults that can be overridden in the local impl.
- [pallet](https://docs.rs/attr.pallet.html)
- The pallet macro has 2 purposes:
- [register_](https://docs.rs/attr.register_default_impl.html)- default_ - impl
- Attach this attribute to an impl statement that you want to use with
`#[derive_impl(..)]`
- [require_](https://docs.rs/attr.require_transactional.html)- transactional
- Assert the annotated function is executed within a storage transaction.
- [runtime](https://docs.rs/attr.runtime.html)
- Construct a runtime, with the given name and the given pallets.
- [storage_](https://docs.rs/attr.storage_alias.html)- alias
- Generate a `#[pallet::storage]`
- [stored](https://docs.rs/attr.stored.html)
- Attribute macro for simplifying storage type definitions with consistent field-based bounding.
- [transactional](https://docs.rs/attr.transactional.html)
- Execute the annotated function in a new storage transaction.

- Derive `Clone`

# frame_system - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/frame-system/^48.0.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#system-pallet)System Pallet

The System pallet provides low-level access to core types and cross-cutting utilities. It acts as the base layer for other pallets to interact with the Substrate framework components.

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

The System pallet defines the core data types used in a Substrate runtime. It also provides
several utility functions (see [ Pallet](https://docs.rs/pallet/struct.Pallet.html)) for other FRAME pallets.

In addition, it manages the storage items for extrinsic data, indices, event records, and digest items, among other things that support the execution of the current block.

It also handles low-level tasks like depositing logs, basic set up and take down of temporary storage entries, and access to previous block hashes.

[§](https://docs.rs#interface)Interface

[§](https://docs.rs#dispatchable-functions)Dispatchable Functions

The System pallet provides dispatchable functions that, with the exception of `remark`, manage
low-level or privileged functionality of a Substrate-based runtime.

- `remark`: Make some on-chain remark.
- `set_heap_pages`: Set the number of pages in the WebAssembly environment’s heap.
- `set_code`: Set the new runtime code.
- `set_code_without_checks`: Set the new runtime code without any checks.
- `set_storage`: Set some items of storage.
- `kill_storage`: Kill some items from storage.
- `kill_prefix`: Kill all storage items with a key that starts with the given prefix.
- `remark_with_event`: Make some on-chain remark and emit an event.
- `do_task`: Do some specified task.
- `authorize_upgrade`: Authorize new runtime code.
- `authorize_upgrade_without_checks`: Authorize new runtime code and an upgrade sans verification.
- `apply_authorized_upgrade`: Provide new, already-authorized runtime code.

[§](https://docs.rs#a-note-on-upgrades)A Note on Upgrades

The pallet provides two primary means of upgrading the runtime, a single-phase means using
`set_code` and a two-phase means using `authorize_upgrade` followed by
`apply_authorized_upgrade`. The first will directly attempt to apply the provided `code`
(application may have to be scheduled, depending on the context and implementation of the
`OnSetCode` trait).

The `authorize_upgrade` route allows the authorization of a runtime’s code hash. Once
authorized, anyone may upload the correct runtime to apply the code. This pattern is useful when
providing the runtime ahead of time may be unwieldy, for example when a large preimage (the
code) would need to be stored on-chain or sent over a message transport protocol such as a
bridge.

The `*_without_checks` variants do not perform any version checks, so using them runs the risk
of applying a downgrade or entirely other chain specification. They will still validate that the
`code` meets the authorized hash.

[§](https://docs.rs#public-functions)Public Functions

See the [ Pallet](https://docs.rs/pallet/struct.Pallet.html) struct for details of publicly available functions.

[§](https://docs.rs#signed-extensions)Signed Extensions

The System pallet defines the following extensions:

- `CheckWeight`
- `CheckNonce`- `T::Nonce`.
- `CheckEra`- `Era`.
- `CheckGenesis`
- `CheckSpecVersion`
- `CheckTxVersion`

Look up the runtime aggregator file (e.g. `node/runtime`) to see the full list of signed
extensions included in a chain.

# pallet_balances - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/pallet-balances/^50.0.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#balances-pallet)Balances Pallet

The Balances pallet provides functionality for handling accounts and balances for a single token.

It makes heavy use of concepts such as Holds and Freezes from the
[ frame_support::traits::fungible](https://docs.rs/frame-support/48.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/frame_support/traits/tokens/fungible/index.html) traits, therefore you should read and understand those docs
as a prerequisite to understanding this pallet.

Also see the [ frame_tokens](https://docs.rs/polkadot_sdk_docs/reference_docs/frame_tokens/index.html) reference docs for higher level information regarding the
place of this palet in FRAME.

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

The Balances pallet provides functions for:

- Getting and setting free balances.
- Retrieving total, reserved and unreserved balances.
- Repatriating a reserved balance to a beneficiary account that exists.
- Transferring a balance between accounts (when not reserved).
- Slashing an account balance.
- Account creation and removal.
- Managing total issuance.
- Setting and managing locks.

[§](https://docs.rs#terminology)Terminology

- **Reaping an account:**The act of removing an account by resetting its nonce. Happens after its total balance has become less than the Existential Deposit.

[§](https://docs.rs#implementations-1)Implementations

The Balances pallet provides implementations for the following [ fungible](https://docs.rs/frame-support/48.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/frame_support/traits/tokens/fungible/index.html) traits. If these
traits provide the functionality that you need, then you should avoid tight coupling with the
Balances pallet.

- `fungible::Inspect`
- `fungible::Mutate`
- `fungible::Unbalanced`
- `fungible::Balanced`
- `fungible::BalancedHold`
- `fungible::InspectHold`
- `fungible::MutateHold`
- `fungible::InspectFreeze`
- `fungible::MutateFreeze`
- `fungible::Imbalance`

It also implements the following [ Currency](https://docs.rs/frame-support/48.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/frame_support/traits/tokens/currency/trait.Currency.html) related traits, however they are deprecated and
will eventually be removed.

- `Currency`
- `ReservableCurrency`
- `NamedReservableCurrency`
- `LockableCurrency`
- `Imbalance`

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The following examples show how to use the Balances pallet in your custom pallet.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-from-the-frame)Examples from the FRAME

The Contract pallet uses the `Currency` trait to handle gas payment, and its types inherit from
`Currency`:

```
use frame_support::traits::Currency;
pub type BalanceOf<T> = <<T as Config>::Currency as Currency<<T as frame_system::Config>::AccountId>>::Balance;
pub type NegativeImbalanceOf<T> = <<T as Config>::Currency as Currency<<T as frame_system::Config>::AccountId>>::NegativeImbalance;
```
The Staking pallet uses the `LockableCurrency` trait to lock a stash account’s funds:

```
use frame_support::traits::{WithdrawReasons, LockableCurrency};
use sp_runtime::traits::Bounded;
pub trait Config: frame_system::Config {
    type Currency: LockableCurrency<Self::AccountId, Moment=frame_system::pallet_prelude::BlockNumberFor<Self>>;
}
fn update_ledger<T: Config>(
    controller: &T::AccountId,
    ledger: &StakingLedger<T>
) {
    T::Currency::set_lock(
        STAKING_ID,
        &ledger.stash,
        ledger.total,
        WithdrawReasons::all()
    );
    // <Ledger<T>>::insert(controller, ledger); // Commented out as we don't have access to Staking's storage here.
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#genesis-config)Genesis config

The Balances pallet depends on the [ GenesisConfig](https://docs.rs/pallet/struct.GenesisConfig.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#assumptions)Assumptions

- Total issued balanced of all accounts should be less than `Config::Balance::max_value()`.
- Existential Deposit is set to a value greater than zero.

Note, you may find the Balances pallet still functions with an ED of zero when the
`insecure_zero_ed` cargo feature is enabled. However this is not a configuration which is
generally supported, nor will it be.

- `pub use`- [pallet](https://docs.rs/pallet/index.html)::*;

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Account](https://docs.rs/struct.AccountData.html)- Data

- [Balance](https://docs.rs/struct.BalanceLock.html)- Lock
- A single lock on a balance. There can be many of these on an account and they “overlap”, so the same balance is frozen by multiple locks.
- [Dust](https://docs.rs/struct.DustCleaner.html)- Cleaner

# pallet_message_queue - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/pallet-message-queue/^52.0.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#generalized-message-queue-pallet)Generalized Message Queue Pallet

Provides generalized message queuing and processing capabilities on a per-queue basis for arbitrary use-cases.

[§](https://docs.rs#design-goals)Design Goals

- Minimal assumptions about `Message`s and`MessageOrigin`s. Both should be MEL bounded blobs. This ensures the generality and reusability of the pallet.
- Well known and tightly limited pre-dispatch PoV weights, especially for message execution.
This is paramount for the success of the pallet since message execution is done in
`on_initialize`which must*never*under-estimate its PoV weight. It also needs a frugal PoV footprint since PoV is scarce and this is (possibly) done in every block. This must also hold in the presence of unpredictable message size distributions.
- Usable as XCMP, DMP and UMP message/dispatch queue - possibly through adapter types.

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

The pallet has means to enqueue, store and process messages. This is implemented by having
*queues* which store enqueued messages and can be *served* to process said messages. A queue is
identified by its origin in the `BookStateFor`. Each message has an origin which defines into
which queue it will be stored. Messages are stored by being appended to the last [ Page](https://docs.rs/struct.Page.html) of a
book. Each book keeps track of its pages by indexing

`Pages`. The `ReadyRing` contains all
queues which hold at least one unprocessed message and are thereby *ready*to be serviced. The

`ServiceHead` indicates which *ready*queue is the next to be serviced. The pallet implements

[,](https://docs.rs/frame-support/48.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/frame_support/traits/messages/trait.EnqueueMessage.html)

`frame_support::traits::EnqueueMessage`[and has](https://docs.rs/frame-support/48.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/frame_support/traits/messages/trait.ServiceQueues.html)

`frame_support::traits::ServiceQueues`[and](https://docs.rs/frame-support/48.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/frame_support/traits/messages/trait.ProcessMessage.html)

`frame_support::traits::ProcessMessage`[hooks to communicate with the outside world.](https://docs.rs/trait.OnQueueChanged.html)

`OnQueueChanged`NOTE: The storage items are not linked since they are not public.

**Message Execution**

Executing a message is offloaded to the [ Config::MessageProcessor](https://docs.rs/pallet/trait.Config.html#associatedtype.MessageProcessor) which contains the actual
logic of how to handle the message since they are blobs. Storage changes are not rolled back on
error.

A failed message can be temporarily or permanently overweight. The pallet will perpetually try to execute a temporarily overweight message. A permanently overweight message is skipped and must be executed manually.

**Reentrancy**

This pallet has two entry points for executing (possibly recursive) logic;
[ Pallet::service_queues](https://docs.rs/pallet/struct.Pallet.html#method.service_queues) and

[. Both entry points are guarded by the same mutex to error on reentrancy. The only functions that are explicitly](https://docs.rs/pallet/struct.Pallet.html#method.execute_overweight)

`Pallet::execute_overweight`**allowed**to be called by a message processor are:

[and](https://docs.rs/pallet/struct.Pallet.html#method.enqueue_message)

`Pallet::enqueue_message`[. All other functions are forbidden and error with](https://docs.rs/pallet/struct.Pallet.html#method.enqueue_messages)

`Pallet::enqueue_messages`[.](https://docs.rs/pallet/enum.Error.html#variant.RecursiveDisallowed)

`Error::RecursiveDisallowed`**Pagination**

Queues are stored in a *paged* manner by splitting their messages into [ Page](https://docs.rs/struct.Page.html)s. This results
in a lot of complexity when implementing the pallet but is completely necessary to achieve the
second #

[Design Goal](https://docs.rs/design-goals). The problem comes from the fact a message can

*possibly*be quite large, lets say 64KiB. This then results in a

*MEL*of at least 64KiB which results in a PoV of at least 64KiB. Now we have the assumption that most messages are much shorter than their maximum allowed length. This would result in most messages having a pre-dispatch PoV size which is much larger than their post-dispatch PoV size, possibly by a factor of thousand. Disregarding this observation would cripple the processing power of the pallet since it cannot straighten out this discrepancy at runtime. Conceptually, the implementation is packing as many messages into a single bounded vec, as actually fit into the bounds. This reduces the wasted PoV.

**Page Data Layout**

A Page contains a heap which holds all its messages. The heap is built by concatenating
`(ItemHeader, Message)` pairs. The [ ItemHeader](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemHeader.html) contains the length of the message which is
needed for retrieving it. This layout allows for constant access time of the next message and
linear access time for any message in the page. The header must remain minimal to reduce its PoV
impact.

**Weight Metering**

The pallet utilizes the [ sp_weights::WeightMeter](https://docs.rs/sp-weights/36.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sp_weights/weight_meter/struct.WeightMeter.html) to manually track its consumption to always
stay within the required limit. This implies that the message processor hook can calculate the
weight of a message without executing it. This restricts the possible use-cases but is necessary
since the pallet runs in

`on_initialize` which has a hard weight limit. The weight meter is used
in a way that `can_accrue` and `check_accrue` are always used to check the remaining weight of
an operation before committing to it. The process of exiting due to insufficient weight is
termed “bailing”.[§](https://docs.rs#scenario-message-enqueuing)Scenario: Message enqueuing

A message `m` is enqueued for origin `o` into queue `Q[o]` through
`frame_support::traits::EnqueueMessage::enqueue_message``(m, o)`.

First the queue is either loaded if it exists or otherwise created with empty default values.
The message is then inserted to the queue by appended it into its last `Page` or by creating a
new `Page` just for `m` if it does not fit in there. The number of messages in the `Book` is
incremented.

`Q[o]` is now *ready* which will eventually result in `m` being processed.

[§](https://docs.rs#scenario-message-processing)Scenario: Message processing

The pallet runs each block in `on_initialize` or when being manually called through
[ frame_support::traits::ServiceQueues::service_queues](https://docs.rs/frame-support/48.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/frame_support/traits/messages/trait.ServiceQueues.html#tymethod.service_queues).

First it tries to “rotate” the `ReadyRing` by one through advancing the `ServiceHead` to the
next *ready* queue. It then starts to service this queue by servicing as many pages of it as
possible. Servicing a page means to execute as many message of it as possible. Each executed
message is marked as *processed* if the [ Config::MessageProcessor](https://docs.rs/pallet/trait.Config.html#associatedtype.MessageProcessor) return Ok. An event

[is emitted afterwards. It is possible that the weight limit of the pallet will never allow a specific message to be executed. In this case it remains as unprocessed and is skipped. This process stops if either there are no more messages in the queue or the remaining weight became insufficient to service this queue. If there is enough weight it tries to advance to the next](https://docs.rs/pallet/enum.Event.html#variant.Processed)

`Event::Processed`*ready*queue and service it. This continues until there are no more queues on which it can make progress or not enough weight to check that.

[§](https://docs.rs#scenario-overweight-execution)Scenario: Overweight execution

A permanently over-weight message which was skipped by the message processing will never be
executed automatically through `on_initialize` nor by calling
[ frame_support::traits::ServiceQueues::service_queues](https://docs.rs/frame-support/48.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/frame_support/traits/messages/trait.ServiceQueues.html#tymethod.service_queues).

Manual intervention in the form of
[ frame_support::traits::ServiceQueues::execute_overweight](https://docs.rs/frame-support/48.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/frame_support/traits/messages/trait.ServiceQueues.html#method.execute_overweight) is necessary. Overweight messages
emit an

[event which can be used to extract the arguments for manual execution. This only works on permanently overweight messages. There is no guarantee that this will work since the message could be part of a stale page and be reaped before execution commences.](https://docs.rs/pallet/enum.Event.html#variant.OverweightEnqueued)

`Event::OverweightEnqueued`[§](https://docs.rs#terminology)Terminology

- `Message`: A blob of data into which the pallet has no introspection, defined as- `BoundedSlice<u8, MaxMessageLenOf<T>>`- `MaxMessageLenOf`- `Config::HeapSize`- `ItemHeader::max_encoded_len()`
- `MessageOrigin`: A generic- *origin*of a message, defined as- `MessageOriginOf`- `frame_support::traits::ProcessMessage::Origin`
- `Page`: An array of- `Message`s, see- `Page`
- `Book`: A list of- `Page`s, see- `BookState`
- `Queue`: A- `Book`together with an- `MessageOrigin`which can be part of the- `ReadyRing`. Can be empty.
- `ReadyRing`: A double-linked list which contains all- *ready*- `Queue`s. It chains together the queues via their- `ready_neighbours`fields. A- `Queue`is- *ready*if it contains at least one- `Message`which can be processed. Can be empty.
- `ServiceHead`: A pointer into the- `ReadyRing`to the next- `Queue`to be serviced.
- (`un`)`processed`: A message is marked as*processed*after it was executed by the pallet. A message which was either: not yet executed or could not be executed remains as`unprocessed`which is the default state for a message after being enqueued.
- `knitting`/- `unknitting`: The means of adding or removing a- `Queue`from the- `ReadyRing`.
- `MEL`: The Max Encoded Length of a type, see- `codec::MaxEncodedLen`
- `Reentrance`: To enter an execution context again before it has completed.

[§](https://docs.rs#properties)Properties

**Liveness - Enqueueing**

It is always possible to enqueue any message for any `MessageOrigin`.

**Liveness - Processing**

`on_initialize` always respects its finite weight-limit.

**Progress - Enqueueing**

An enqueued message immediately becomes *unprocessed* and thereby eligible for execution.

**Progress - Processing**

The pallet will execute at least one unprocessed message per block, if there is any. Ensuring
this property needs careful consideration of the concrete weights, since it is possible that the
weight limit of `on_initialize` never allows for the execution of even one message; trivially if
the limit is set to zero. `integrity_test` can be used to ensure that this property holds.

**Fairness - Enqueuing**

Enqueueing a message for a specific `MessageOrigin` does not influence the ability to enqueue a
message for the same of any other `MessageOrigin`; guaranteed by **Liveness - Enqueueing**.

**Fairness - Processing**

The average amount of weight available for message processing is the same for each queue if the
number of queues is constant. Creating a new queue must therefore be, possibly economically,
expensive. Currently this is archived by having one queue per para-chain/thread, which keeps the
number of queues within `O(n)` and should be “good enough”.

# pallet_timestamp - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/pallet-timestamp/^48.0.0/

## Expand description

Made with

Substrate, forPolkadot.

[§](https://docs.rs#timestamp-pallet)Timestamp Pallet

A pallet that provides a way for consensus systems to set and check the onchain time.

[§](https://docs.rs#pallet-api)Pallet API

See the [ pallet](https://docs.rs/pallet/index.html) module for more information about the interfaces this pallet exposes,
including its configuration trait, dispatchables, storage items, events and errors.

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

The Timestamp pallet is designed to create a consensus-based time source. This helps ensure that nodes maintain a synchronized view of time that all network participants can agree on.

It defines an *acceptable range* using a configurable constant to specify how much time must
pass before setting the new timestamp. Validator nodes in the network must verify that the
timestamp falls within this acceptable range and reject blocks that do not.

Note:The timestamp set by this pallet is the recommended way to query the onchain time instead of using block numbers alone. Measuring time with block numbers can cause cumulative calculation errors if depended upon in time critical operations and hence should generally be avoided.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

To get the current time for the current block in another pallet:

```
use pallet_timestamp::{self as timestamp};
#[frame_support::pallet]
pub mod pallet {
	use super::*;
	use frame_support::pallet_prelude::*;
	use frame_system::pallet_prelude::*;
	#[pallet::pallet]
	pub struct Pallet<T>(_);
	#[pallet::config]
	pub trait Config: frame_system::Config + timestamp::Config {}
	#[pallet::call]
	impl<T: Config> Pallet<T> {
		#[pallet::weight(0)]
		pub fn get_time(origin: OriginFor<T>) -> DispatchResult {
			let _sender = ensure_signed(origin)?;
			let _now = timestamp::Pallet::<T>::get();
			Ok(())
		}
	}
}
```
If [ Pallet::get](https://docs.rs/pallet/struct.Pallet.html#method.get) is called prior to setting the timestamp, it will return the timestamp of
the previous block.

[§](https://docs.rs#low-level--implementation-details)Low Level / Implementation Details

A timestamp is added to the chain using an *inherent extrinsic* that only a block author can
submit. Inherents are a special type of extrinsic in Substrate chains that will always be
included in a block.

To provide inherent data to the runtime, this pallet implements
[ ProvideInherent](https://docs.rs/frame-support/48.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/frame_support/inherent/trait.ProvideInherent.html). It will only create an inherent
if the

[dispatchable is called, using the](https://docs.rs/pallet/enum.Call.html#variant.set)

`Call::set`[macro which enables validator nodes to call into the runtime to check that the timestamp provided is valid. The implementation of](https://docs.rs/frame-support-procedural/40.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/frame_support_procedural/attr.inherent.html)

`inherent`[specifies a constant called](https://docs.rs/frame-support/48.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/frame_support/inherent/trait.ProvideInherent.html)

`ProvideInherent``MAX_TIMESTAMP_DRIFT_MILLIS` which is used to determine the acceptable range for
a valid timestamp. If a block author sets a timestamp to anything that is more than this
constant, a validator node will reject the block.The pallet also ensures that a timestamp is set at the start of each block by running an
assertion in the `on_finalize` runtime hook. See [ frame_support::traits::Hooks](https://docs.rs/frame-support/48.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/frame_support/traits/hooks/trait.Hooks.html) for more
information about how hooks work.

Because inherents are applied to a block in the order they appear in the runtime
construction, the index of this pallet in
[ construct_runtime](https://docs.rs/frame-support-procedural/40.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/frame_support_procedural/macro.construct_runtime.html) must always be less than any other
pallet that depends on it.

The [ Config::OnTimestampSet](https://docs.rs/pallet/trait.Config.html#associatedtype.OnTimestampSet) configuration trait can be set to another pallet we want to
notify that the timestamp has been updated, as long as it implements

[. Examples are the Babe and Aura pallets. This pallet also implements](https://docs.rs/frame-support/48.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/frame_support/traits/hooks/trait.OnTimestampSet.html)

`OnTimestampSet`[and](https://docs.rs/frame-support/48.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/frame_support/traits/misc/trait.Time.html)

`Time`[so it can be used to configure other pallets that require these types (e.g. in Staking pallet).](https://docs.rs/frame-support/48.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/frame_support/traits/misc/trait.UnixTime.html)

`UnixTime`[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

There are 3 cases where this pallet could cause the runtime to panic.

-
If no timestamp is set at the end of a block.
-
If a timestamp is set more than once per block:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[test]
#[should_panic(expected = "Timestamp must be updated only once in the block")]
fn double_timestamp_should_fail() {
	new_test_ext().execute_with(|| {
		Timestamp::set_timestamp(42);
		assert_ok!(Timestamp::set(RuntimeOrigin::none(), 69));
	});
}
```
- If a timestamp is set before the `Config::MinimumPeriod`

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[test]
#[should_panic(
	expected = "Timestamp must increment by at least <MinimumPeriod> between sequential blocks"
)]
fn block_period_minimum_enforced() {
	new_test_ext().execute_with(|| {
		crate::Now::<Test>::put(44);
		let _ = Timestamp::set(RuntimeOrigin::none(), 46);
	});
}
```
## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use weights::`- [WeightInfo](https://docs.rs/weights/trait.WeightInfo.html);
- `pub use`- [pallet](https://docs.rs/pallet/index.html)::*;

# paste - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/paste/^1.0.15/

## Expand description

The nightly-only [ concat_idents!](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/macro.concat_idents.html) macro in the Rust standard library is
notoriously underpowered in that its concatenated identifiers can only refer to
existing items, they can never be used to define something new.

This crate provides a flexible way to paste together identifiers in a macro, including using pasted identifiers to define new items.

This approach works with any Rust compiler 1.31+.

[§](https://docs.rs#pasting-identifiers)Pasting identifiers

Within the `paste!` macro, identifiers inside `[<`…`>]` are pasted
together to form a single identifier.

```
use paste::paste;
paste! {
    // Defines a const called `QRST`.
    const [<Q R S T>]: &str = "success!";
}
fn main() {
    assert_eq!(
        paste! { [<Q R S T>].len() },
        8,
    );
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#more-elaborate-example)More elaborate example

The next example shows a macro that generates accessor methods for some struct fields. It demonstrates how you might find it useful to bundle a paste invocation inside of a macro_rules macro.

```
use paste::paste;
macro_rules! make_a_struct_and_getters {
    ($name:ident { $($field:ident),* }) => {
        // Define a struct. This expands to:
        //
        //     pub struct S {
        //         a: String,
        //         b: String,
        //         c: String,
        //     }
        pub struct $name {
            $(
                $field: String,
            )*
        }
        // Build an impl block with getters. This expands to:
        //
        //     impl S {
        //         pub fn get_a(&self) -> &str { &self.a }
        //         pub fn get_b(&self) -> &str { &self.b }
        //         pub fn get_c(&self) -> &str { &self.c }
        //     }
        paste! {
            impl $name {
                $(
                    pub fn [<get_ $field>](&self) -> &str {
                        &self.$field
                    }
                )*
            }
        }
    }
}
make_a_struct_and_getters!(S { a, b, c });
fn call_some_getters(s: &S) -> bool {
    s.get_a() == s.get_b() && s.get_c().is_empty()
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#case-conversion)Case conversion

Use `$var:lower` or `$var:upper` in the segment list to convert an
interpolated segment to lower- or uppercase as part of the paste. For
example, `[<ld_ $reg:lower _expr>]` would paste to `ld_bc_expr` if invoked
with $reg=`Bc`.

Use `$var:snake` to convert CamelCase input to snake_case.
Use `$var:camel` to convert snake_case to CamelCase.
These compose, so for example `$var:snake:upper` would give you SCREAMING_CASE.

The precise Unicode conversions are as defined by [ str::to_lowercase](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html#method.to_lowercase) and

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html#method.to_uppercase)

`str::to_uppercase`[§](https://docs.rs#pasting-documentation-strings)Pasting documentation strings

Within the `paste!` macro, arguments to a #[doc …] attribute are
implicitly concatenated together to form a coherent documentation string.

```
use paste::paste;
macro_rules! method_new {
    ($ret:ident) => {
        paste! {
            #[doc = "Create a new `" $ret "` object."]
            pub fn new() -> $ret { todo!() }
        }
    };
}
pub struct Paste {}
method_new!(Paste);  // expands to #[doc = "Create a new `Paste` object"]
```

---

# polkadot_parachain_primitives - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/polkadot-parachain-primitives/^23.0.0/

## Expand description

Defines primitive types for creating or validating a parachain.

When compiled with standard library support, this crate exports a `wasm`
module that can be used to validate parachain WASM.

[§](https://docs.rs#parachain-wasm)Parachain WASM

Polkadot parachain WASM is in the form of a module which imports a memory
instance and exports a function `validate_block`.

`validate` accepts as input two `i32` values, representing a pointer/length pair
respectively, that encodes [ ValidationParams](https://docs.rs/primitives/struct.ValidationParams.html).

`validate` returns an `u64` which is a pointer to an `u8` array and its length.
The data in the array is expected to be a SCALE encoded
[ ValidationResult](https://docs.rs/primitives/struct.ValidationResult.html).

ASCII-diagram demonstrating the return data format:

The wasm-api (enabled only when `std` feature is not enabled and `wasm-api` feature is enabled)
provides utilities for setting up a parachain WASM module in Rust.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [primitives](https://docs.rs/primitives/index.html)
- Primitive types which are strictly necessary from a parachain-execution point of view.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Blake](https://docs.rs/struct.BlakeTwo256.html)- Two256
- Blake2-256 Hash implementation.
- [Candidate](https://docs.rs/struct.CandidateHash.html)- Hash
- Unit type wrapper around `Hash`
- [Head](https://docs.rs/struct.HeadData.html)- Data
- Parachain head data included in the chain.
- [Hrmp](https://docs.rs/struct.HrmpChannelId.html)- Channel - Id
- A type that uniquely identifies an HRMP channel. An HRMP channel is established between two
paras. In text, we use the notation `(A, B)`to specify a channel between A and B. The channels are unidirectional, meaning that`(A, B)`and`(B, A)`refer to different channels. The convention is that we use the first item tuple for the sender and the second for the recipient. Only one channel is allowed between two participants in one direction, i.e. there cannot be 2 different channels identified by`(A, B)`. A channel with the same para id in sender and recipient is invalid. That is, however, not enforced.
- [Id](https://docs.rs/struct.Id.html)
- Unique identifier of a parachain.
- [Inbound](https://docs.rs/struct.InboundDownwardMessage.html)- Downward - Message
- A wrapped version of `DownwardMessage`. The difference is that it has attached the block number when the message was sent.
- [Inbound](https://docs.rs/struct.InboundHrmpMessage.html)- Hrmp - Message
- An HRMP message seen from the perspective of a recipient.
- [Outbound](https://docs.rs/struct.OutboundHrmpMessage.html)- Hrmp - Message
- An HRMP message seen from the perspective of a sender.
- [Slot](https://docs.rs/struct.Slot.html)
- Unit type wrapper that represents a slot.
- [Validation](https://docs.rs/struct.ValidationCode.html)- Code
- Parachain validation code.
- [Validation](https://docs.rs/struct.ValidationCodeHash.html)- Code - Hash
- Unit type wrapper around `Hash`

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [LOWEST_](https://docs.rs/constant.LOWEST_PUBLIC_ID.html)- PUBLIC_ - ID
- The ID of the first publicly registrable parachain.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- Abstraction around hashing

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Account](https://docs.rs/type.AccountId.html)- Id
- Alias to the opaque account ID type for this chain, actually a `AccountId32`. This is always 32 bytes.
- [Account](https://docs.rs/type.AccountIndex.html)- Index
- The type for looking up accounts. We don’t expect more than 4 billion of them.
- [Account](https://docs.rs/type.AccountPublic.html)- Public
- Alias to the public key used for this chain, actually a `MultiSigner`. Like the signature, this also isn’t a fixed size when encoded, as different cryptos have different size public keys.
- [Authority](https://docs.rs/type.AuthorityDiscoveryId.html)- Discovery - Id
- An authority discovery authority identifier.
- [Balance](https://docs.rs/type.Balance.html)
- The balance of an account.
128-bits (or 38 significant decimal figures) will allow for 10 m currency (`10^7`) at a resolution to all for one second’s worth of an annualised 50% reward be paid to a unit holder (`10^11`unit denomination), or`10^18`total atomic units, to grow at 50%/year for 51 years (`10^9`multiplier) for an eventual total of`10^27`units (27 significant decimal figures). We round denomination to`10^12`(12 SDF), and leave the other redundancy at the upper end so that 32 bits may be multiplied with a balance in 128 bits without worrying about overflow.
- [Block](https://docs.rs/type.Block.html)
- Block type.
- [BlockId](https://docs.rs/type.BlockId.html)
- Block ID.
- [Block](https://docs.rs/type.BlockNumber.html)- Number
- The block number type used by Polkadot. 32-bits will allow for 136 years of blocks assuming 1 block per second.
- [Downward](https://docs.rs/type.DownwardMessage.html)- Message
- A message sent from the relay-chain down to a parachain.
- [Hash](https://docs.rs/type.Hash.html)
- A hash of some data used by the relay chain.
- [Header](https://docs.rs/type.Header.html)
- Header type.
- [Horizontal](https://docs.rs/type.HorizontalMessages.html)- Messages
- [Moment](https://docs.rs/type.Moment.html)
- An instant or duration in time.
- [Nonce](https://docs.rs/type.Nonce.html)
- Index of a transaction in the relay chain. 32-bit should be plenty.
- [Session](https://docs.rs/type.SessionIndex.html)- Index
- Simple index type with which we can count sessions.
- [Signature](https://docs.rs/type.Signature.html)
- Alias to type for a signature for a transaction on the relay chain. This allows one of several kinds of underlying crypto to be used, so isn’t a fixed size when encoded.
- [Upward](https://docs.rs/type.UpwardMessage.html)- Message
- A message from a parachain to its Relay Chain.

# polkadot_runtime_parachains - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/polkadot-runtime-parachains/^28.0.0/

## Expand description

Runtime modules for parachains code.

It is crucial to include all the modules from this crate in the runtime, in
particular the `Initializer` module, as it is responsible for initializing the state
of the other modules.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use origin::`- [ensure_parachain](https://docs.rs/origin/fn.ensure_parachain.html);
- `pub use origin::`- [Origin](https://docs.rs/origin/pallet/enum.Origin.html);
- `pub use paras::`- [ParaLifecycle](https://docs.rs/paras/enum.ParaLifecycle.html);
- `pub use paras::`- [UpgradeStrategy](https://docs.rs/paras/enum.UpgradeStrategy.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [configuration](https://docs.rs/configuration/index.html)
- Configuration manager for the Polkadot runtime parachains logic.
- [coretime](https://docs.rs/coretime/index.html)
- This pallet exposes the relay chain coretime functionality to the broker/coretime chain.
- [disputes](https://docs.rs/disputes/index.html)
- Runtime component for handling disputes of parachain candidates.
- [dmp](https://docs.rs/dmp/index.html)
- To prevent Out of Memory errors on the `DownwardMessageQueue`, an exponential fee factor (`DeliveryFeeFactor`) is set. The fee factor increments exponentially after the number of messages in the`DownwardMessageQueue`passes a threshold. This threshold is set as:
- [hrmp](https://docs.rs/hrmp/index.html)
- [inclusion](https://docs.rs/inclusion/index.html)
- The inclusion pallet is responsible for inclusion and availability of scheduled parachains.
- [initializer](https://docs.rs/initializer/index.html)
- This module is responsible for maintaining a consistent initialization order for all other parachains modules. It’s also responsible for finalization and session change notifications.
- [metrics](https://docs.rs/metrics/index.html)
- Runtime declaration of the parachain metrics.
- [on_](https://docs.rs/on_demand/index.html)- demand
- The parachain on demand assignment module.
- [origin](https://docs.rs/origin/index.html)
- Declaration of the parachain specific origin and a pallet that hosts it.
- [paras](https://docs.rs/paras/index.html)
- The paras pallet acts as the main registry of paras.
- [paras_](https://docs.rs/paras_inherent/index.html)- inherent
- Provides glue code over the scheduler and inclusion modules, and accepting one inherent per block that can include new para candidates and bitfields.
- [reward_](https://docs.rs/reward_points/index.html)- points
- An implementation of the `RewardValidators`trait used by`inclusion`that employs`pallet-staking`to compute the rewards.
- [runtime_](https://docs.rs/runtime_api_impl/index.html)- api_ - impl
- Runtime API implementations for Parachains.
- [scheduler](https://docs.rs/scheduler/index.html)
- The scheduler module for parachains and parathreads.
- [session_](https://docs.rs/session_info/index.html)- info
- The session info pallet provides information about validator sets from prior sessions needed for approvals and disputes.
- [shared](https://docs.rs/shared/index.html)
- A pallet for any shared state that other pallets may want access to.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [GetMin](https://docs.rs/struct.GetMinFeeFactor.html)- FeeFactor
- Helper struct used for accessing `FeeTracker::MIN_FEE_FACTOR`

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [FeeTracker](https://docs.rs/trait.FeeTracker.html)
- Trait for tracking message delivery fees on a transport protocol.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [schedule_](https://docs.rs/fn.schedule_code_upgrade.html)- code_ - upgrade
- Schedules a validation code upgrade to a parachain with the given id.
- [schedule_](https://docs.rs/fn.schedule_para_cleanup.html)- para_ - cleanup
- Schedule a para to be cleaned up at the start of the next session.
- [schedule_](https://docs.rs/fn.schedule_para_initialize.html)- para_ - initialize
- Schedule a para to be initialized at the start of the next session with the given genesis data.
- [schedule_](https://docs.rs/fn.schedule_parachain_downgrade.html)- parachain_ - downgrade
- Schedule a lease holding parachain to be downgraded to an on-demand parachain.
- [schedule_](https://docs.rs/fn.schedule_parathread_upgrade.html)- parathread_ - upgrade
- Schedule a parathread (on-demand parachain) to be upgraded to a lease holding parachain.
- [set_](https://docs.rs/fn.set_current_head.html)- current_ - head
- Sets the current parachain head with the given id.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [biguint](https://docs.rs/biguint/index.html)
- Infinite precision unsigned integer for substrate runtime.
- [fixed_](https://docs.rs/fixed_point/index.html)- point
- Decimal Fixed Point implementations for Substrate runtime.
Similar to types that implement `PerThing`
- [helpers_](https://docs.rs/helpers_128bit/index.html)- 128bit
- Some helper functions to work with 128bit numbers. Note that the functionality provided here is only sensible to use with 128bit numbers because for smaller sizes, you can always rely on assumptions of a bigger type (u128) being available, or simply create a per-thing and use the multiplication implementation provided there.
- [per_](https://docs.rs/per_things/index.html)- things
- Types that implement `PerThing``[0, 1]`. The primary types may you encounter in Substrate would be the following:
- [rational](https://docs.rs/rational/index.html)
- [traits](https://docs.rs/traits/index.html)
- Primitive traits for the runtime arithmetic.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [bounded_](https://docs.rs/bounded_btree_map/index.html)- btree_ - map
- Traits, types and structs to support a bounded BTreeMap.
- [bounded_](https://docs.rs/bounded_vec/index.html)- vec
- Traits, types and structs to support putting a bounded vector into storage, as a raw value, map or a double map.
- [const_](https://docs.rs/const_hex2array/index.html)- hex2array
- Provides a const function for converting a hex string to a `u8`array at compile time, when used in the proper context.
- [crypto](https://docs.rs/crypto/index.html)
- Cryptographic utilities.
- [crypto_](https://docs.rs/crypto_bytes/index.html)- bytes
- Generic byte array which can be specialized with a marker type.
- [defer](https://docs.rs/defer/index.html)
- Contains the `crate::defer!`*deferring*the execution of code until the current scope is dropped. This helps with*always*executing cleanup code.
- [ecdsa](https://docs.rs/ecdsa/index.html)
- Simple ECDSA secp256k1 API.
- [ed25519](https://docs.rs/ed25519/index.html)
- Simple Ed25519 API.
- [hash](https://docs.rs/hash/index.html)
- A fixed hash type.
- [hexdisplay](https://docs.rs/hexdisplay/index.html)
- Wrapper type for byte collections that outputs hex.

# sp_io - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sp-io/^48.0.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#substrate-primitives-io)Substrate Primitives: IO

This crate contains interfaces for the runtime to communicate with the outside world, ergo `io`.
In other context, such interfaces are referred to as “**host functions**”.

Each set of host functions are defined with an instance of the
[ sp_runtime_interface::runtime_interface](https://docs.rs/sp-runtime-interface-proc-macro/21.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sp_runtime_interface_proc_macro/attr.runtime_interface.html) macro.

Most notably, this crate contains host functions for:

All of the default host functions provided by this crate, and by default contained in all
substrate-based clients are amalgamated in [ SubstrateHostFunctions](https://docs.rs/type.SubstrateHostFunctions.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#externalities)Externalities

Host functions go hand in hand with the concept of externalities. Externalities are an environment in which host functions are provided, and thus can be accessed. Some host functions are only accessible in an externality environment that provides it.

A typical error for substrate developers is the following:

This code will panic with the following error:

`thread 'main' panicked at '`get_version_1` called outside of an Externalities-provided environment.'`Such error messages should always be interpreted as “code accessing host functions accessed outside of externalities”.

An externality is any type that implements [ sp_externalities::Externalities](https://docs.rs/sp-externalities/0.34.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sp_externalities/trait.Externalities.html). A simple example
of which is

[, which is commonly used in tests and is exported from this crate.](https://docs.rs/type.TestExternalities.html)

`TestExternalities````
use sp_io::{storage::get, TestExternalities};
TestExternalities::default().execute_with(|| {
	let data = get(b"hello world");
});
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [allocator](https://docs.rs/allocator/index.html)
- Wasm only interface that provides functions for calling into the allocator.
- [crypto](https://docs.rs/crypto/index.html)
- Interfaces for working with crypto related types from within the runtime.
- [default_](https://docs.rs/default_child_storage/index.html)- child_ - storage
- Interface for accessing the child storage for default child trie, from within the runtime.
- [hashing](https://docs.rs/hashing/index.html)
- Interface that provides functions for hashing with different algorithms.
- [logging](https://docs.rs/logging/index.html)
- Interface that provides functions for logging from within the runtime.
- [misc](https://docs.rs/misc/index.html)
- Interface that provides miscellaneous functions for communicating between the runtime and the node.
- [offchain](https://docs.rs/offchain/index.html)
- Interface that provides functions to access the offchain functionality.
- [offchain_](https://docs.rs/offchain_index/index.html)- index
- Interface that provides functions to access the Offchain DB.
- [panic_](https://docs.rs/panic_handler/index.html)- handler
- WASM-only interface which allows for aborting the execution in case of an unrecoverable error.
- [storage](https://docs.rs/storage/index.html)
- Interface for accessing the storage from within the runtime.
- [transaction_](https://docs.rs/transaction_index/index.html)- index
- Interface that provides transaction indexing API.
- [trie](https://docs.rs/trie/index.html)
- Interface that provides trie related functionality.
- [wasm_](https://docs.rs/wasm_tracing/index.html)- tracing
- Interface to provide tracing facilities for wasm. Modelled after tokios `tracing`-crate interfaces. See`sp-tracing`for more information.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Multi](https://docs.rs/struct.MultiRemovalResults.html)- Removal - Results
- Results concerning an operation to remove many keys.
- [UseDalek](https://docs.rs/struct.UseDalekExt.html)- Ext
- Extension to signal to [`crypt::ed25519_verify`] to use the dalek crate.

- Error verifying ECDSA signature
- [Kill](https://docs.rs/enum.KillStorageResult.html)- Storage - Result
- The outcome of calling `storage_kill`. Returned value is the number of storage items removed from the backend from making the`storage_kill`call.

- Initialize tracing of sp_tracing not necessary – noop. To enable build

# sp_runtime - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sp-runtime/^48.0.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#substrate-runtime-primitives)Substrate Runtime Primitives.

This crate, among other things, contains a large library of types and utilities that are used in
the Substrate runtime, but are not particularly `FRAME`-oriented.

[§](https://docs.rs#block-header-and-extrinsics)Block, Header and Extrinsics

Most notable, this crate contains some of the types and trait that enable important communication between the client and the runtime. This includes:

- A set of traits to declare what any block/header/extrinsic type should provide.
- A set of types that implement these traits, whilst still providing a high degree of configurability via generics.

[§](https://docs.rs#runtime-api-types)Runtime API Types

This crate also contains some types that are often used in conjuncture with Runtime APIs. Most notable:

- `ApplyExtrinsicResult`- `DispatchOutcome`
- `transaction_validity`

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use generic::`- [Digest](https://docs.rs/generic/struct.Digest.html);
- `pub use generic::`- [DigestItem](https://docs.rs/generic/enum.DigestItem.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [biguint](https://docs.rs/biguint/index.html)
- Re-export big_uint stuff. Infinite precision unsigned integer for substrate runtime.
- [bounded_](https://docs.rs/bounded_btree_map/index.html)- btree_ - map
- Re-export bounded_vec and bounded_btree_map macros only when std is enabled. Traits, types and structs to support a bounded BTreeMap.
- [bounded_](https://docs.rs/bounded_vec/index.html)- vec
- Re-export bounded_vec and bounded_btree_map macros only when std is enabled. Traits, types and structs to support putting a bounded vector into storage, as a raw value, map or a double map.
- [curve](https://docs.rs/curve/index.html)
- Provides some utilities to define a piecewise linear function.
- [generic](https://docs.rs/generic/index.html)
- Generic implementations of `crate::traits::Header``crate::traits::Block``crate::traits::ExtrinsicLike`
- [helpers_](https://docs.rs/helpers_128bit/index.html)- 128bit
- Re-export 128 bit helpers. Some helper functions to work with 128bit numbers. Note that the functionality provided here is only sensible to use with 128bit numbers because for smaller sizes, you can always rely on assumptions of a bigger type (u128) being available, or simply create a per-thing and use the multiplication implementation provided there.
- [key_](https://docs.rs/key_types/index.html)- types
- Re-export this since it’s part of the API of this crate. Known key types; this also functions as a global registry of key types for projects wishing to avoid collisions with each other.
- [legacy](https://docs.rs/legacy/index.html)
- Runtime types that existed in old API versions.
- [offchain](https://docs.rs/offchain/index.html)
- A collection of higher lever helpers for offchain calls.
- [proving_](https://docs.rs/proving_trie/index.html)- trie
- Types for merkle tries compatible with the runtime.
- [runtime_](https://docs.rs/runtime_logger/index.html)- logger
- A logger that can be used to log from the runtime.
- [testing](https://docs.rs/testing/index.html)
- Testing utilities.
- [traits](https://docs.rs/traits/index.html)
- Primitives for the runtime modules.
- [transaction_](https://docs.rs/transaction_validity/index.html)- validity
- Transaction validity interface.
- [type_](https://docs.rs/type_with_default/index.html)- with_ - default
- Provides a type that wraps another type and provides a default value.

# sp_tracing - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sp-tracing/^19.0.0/

## Expand description

Substrate tracing primitives and macros.

To trace functions or individual code in Substrate, this crate provides [ within_span](https://docs.rs/macro.within_span.html)
and

[. See the individual docs for how to use these macros.](https://docs.rs/macro.enter_span.html)

`enter_span`Note that to allow traces from wasm execution environment there are
2 reserved identifiers for tracing `Field` recording, stored in the consts:
`WASM_TARGET_KEY` and `WASM_NAME_KEY` - if you choose to record fields, you
must ensure that your identifiers do not clash with either of these.

Additionally, we have a const: `WASM_TRACE_IDENTIFIER`, which holds a span name used
to signal that the ‘actual’ span name and target should be retrieved instead from
the associated Fields mentioned above.

Note: The `tracing` crate requires trace metadata to be static. This does not work
for wasm code in substrate, as it is regularly updated with new code from on-chain
events. The workaround for this is for the wasm tracing wrappers to put the
`name` and `target` data in the `values` map (normally they would be in the static
metadata assembled at compile time).
